Did not enjoy this movie. I was not emotionally moved by anything happening, I wanted to see some baseball action and there was hardly any. All based on the back of house administration processes involved with creating codes that analyze baseball player statistics. The movie was also unnecessarily long and slow-paced. Main character (Brad Pitt) was extremely unlikable and didn’t have many redeeming qualities in my opinion (besides the fact that he had faith in Jonah Hill). Would not watch again or recommend to others, but I’m also not a huge baseball fan so maybe if I was more into baseball I would have liked the movie more.

Moneyball is a sports drama about a baseball manager who uses statistics to build a competitive team with a limited budget. Brad Pitt gives a strong performance and makes the main character charismatic and easy to follow. The film has a realistic style and presents an interesting approach to baseball. However, the story can feel slow and overly focused on statistics and strategy. Some characters lack depth, making it difficult to become emotionally invested in the team. The dialogue is good, but the movie does not create enough excitement outside the baseball world. Overall, it is a well-made sports drama, but I found it rather dull and underwhelming.

asked camille to put this on at 10pm knowing i’d fall asleep and because i wanted to be put to sleep after a weird night emotionally (and there’s no writer who lulls me into somnambulatory hazes more than sorkin, see my myriad attempts to watch the social network that see me snoozing before garfield even gets to say the line about his prada being at the cleaners) and it worked, though i strangely was able to stay awake until damn near an hour twenty with this one and between that and the tens of clips of this i’ve seen during some time-wasting endeavor or another on short-form video applications in the last five+ years i think i’ve metabolized a percentage of the meaningful content of this film that’d be tantamount to a high-A letter-grade. in dearborn, michigan there’s a horrific acres-sprawling henry ford vanity project/oversized and undercontexted memorial, where ford himself picked up and moved edison’s actual lab/residence among other architectural objects important to the late-19th–early-20th centuries’ histories (which despite its obvious odiousness is at least appreciable in the way it’s essentially a super-sized and un-concealed in its greed version of the pillaging drive of all first-world museums, the bareness of it heightening these innate contradictions in a way that’s at least interesting to think about) assumedly as a way of creating a huge synecdoche of america that southeast michigan soon-to-be factory worker children could free roam around and think about the majesty of american ingenuity and invention. during the baseball season there were weekly games where crashed-out/aging minor league players would play baseball as close as possible to how it was played in the 1800s (for the record there were some black players who participated in this but don’t think it’s lost on me or likely the players that this was the specific time period they were tasked to replicate). my dad has a distant but oft-professed love of baseball, and would take our family to sit on the grass on the hill near third-base and eat cold sandwiches and cape cod potato chips and drink izzes sometimes in the summers, an activity that none of us enjoyed or got much out of except him. and while we were sitting there he’d get romantic about baseball as this monument to american cynicism and rugged-if-not-horrific individualism/single-mindedness, how it’s great because most of the gamesmanship happens off the field (either through direct cheating a la the world series fix gatsby is implicated in or the indirect underhanded tactics on display in this movie) but that ultimately it is a game played in real time with so many uncontrolled variables so as to make the thing always feel very alive despite its conceits. i think these descriptions are a lot of the reason i came to love racing so much in my adulthood, the vast team-wide conspiracies required to pull-off certain tech violations (see jeremy clarkson’s tale of lancia tricking fia officials into thinking they’d homologated twice as many 037s as they did , a story that always struck me as a real john hanley classic) or the way that back in the 80s team principles would run any fuel with any additive so long as it made the car faster even if it made the flames invisible as pit-crew-members burned to death. as vulgar and horrific as that level of avarice can be to witness, there’s something i love and find difficult to look away from in all of it. but it should be noted from the eras of sport my dad and now i show interest in that neither of the aforementioned activities really function like that anymore, or at least the stakes are lower and more controlled, and this stakeslessness is why i think my dad found it difficult to care about the period of baseball described in moneyball and why i find it hard to care about hamilton joining ferrari (next season guys i promise). sorkin does an okay job at filling this movie with chewy people-in-rooms dialogue and the director coaxes some decent performances from pitt, hoffman and hill, and sorkin at least has similar thoughts about the game as my dad in a way that made me feel tenderly enough to write this very long review about a movie i was asleep for part of, but he seldom-if-ever works to illustrate why baseball is still a game worthy of keeping his or my father’s rapt attention and in that failure this movie ends up pretty dead on arrival, dead especially because if anyone could be convinced the conniving magic is still there in sport it’s me. but hey, fun movie to fall asleep to and it’s one of the few movies recently that really made me want to have kids without the kid in question being a literal infant–toddler, so it wasn’t for nothing.

Having read on more than one occasion—though the exact sources now escape me—that this was actually the best sports film made yet, I went in with reasonably high expectations. Instead, I should’ve taken these (men’s!!!) opinions with a grain of salt, because this movie sucked. Sports movies are fun because of their homoerotic subtext and the collective simplistic goal of a cookie-cutter victory—but to make money said victory, and to remove the “team” character and instead replace it by self-serving, money-hungry unremarkable men, makes me think of this film as a charmless dollar-store version of The Big Short (2015). And yes, I know it came out four years prior.
